sections.section: Money has a time dimension
sections.lecture_material: 100 rupees today or in one year; rational answer today because of earning power (5% gives 105); money has a time dimension; the rule that cash flows must be moved to the same point in time before comparing or adding (slide f0023, 5 inches and 5 centimetres); cash flows; time value of money.
sections.teaching_construction: Time measured in years from t = 0 and the stated period; the running case (fee of 600,000 rupees at t = 4, an invented 8%, four questions); the three objects (deposit, date, growth function); the rounding rule with the example 600,000 x 0.735030.

sections.section: The amount function and the accumulation function
sections.lecture_material: Principal k at t = 0; amount function A(t) with units of currency (trap alert); accumulation function a(t) for 1 unit, no units, a multiplier (trap alert); scaling equation A(t) = k a(t) assuming linearity of principal (investing 200 gives 2x investing 100); larger rates for larger deposits exist and are not treated; boundary condition a(0) = 1.
sections.teaching_construction: a(t) = A(t)/A(0); the notation collision of a(t) with later annuity symbols stated; the running case as k = 600,000/a(4).

sections.section: Interest earned in a period
sections.lecture_material: Interest is the change in accumulated value over a period; I_n = A(n) - A(n-1) for period n from n-1 to n; trap alert: I_n is an amount, not the rate i.
sections.teaching_construction: The telescoping sum I_1 + ... + I_n = A(n) - A(0) and its no-withdrawal condition; the choice of balance as what separates i from d.

sections.section: The effective rate of interest
sections.lecture_material: Effective rate i = (A(1) - A(0))/A(0) = I_1/A(0) (f0016); trap alert: i is a decimal (5% = 0.05); example 100 to 110, i = 0.10; normalised principal a(0) = 1, i = a(1) - 1, a(1) = 1 + i, the same for simple and compound at t = 1 (f0020).
sections.teaching_construction: Definition of i_n for every period n (1.3) and its independence of k under (1.1); i as the first-period rate for a stated period length; the remark that the definition says nothing about i_2 versus i_1.

sections.section: Simple interest: linear growth
sections.lecture_material: Interest only on the original principal; 100 at 5%: 105, 110, 100(1 + rn) (handwritten f0048 with r); a(t) = 1 + it, constant growth per period, straight line from (0, 1) (f0050).
sections.teaching_construction: Running case simple reading 454,545.45 and yearly interest 36,363.64; the product inequality (1 + is)(1 + it) > 1 + i(s+t) and the renewal gain 618,404.07 (18,404.07 above the fee).

sections.section: Compound interest: exponential growth
sections.lecture_material: Interest on the accumulated balance; 100 at 5%: 105, 110.25 (interest 5.25), 100(1+i)^(n-1)(1+i) = 100(1+i)^n; a(t) = (1+i)^t (f0058); visual comparison with a widening gap (f0060); preview of the trap for 0 < t < 1.
sections.teaching_construction: Fractional-time compound growth stated as the model's definition; the product rule a(s+t) = a(s)a(t); running case compound reading 441,017.91, balances and yearly interest.

sections.section: The effective rate over time: constant for compound, falling for simple
sections.lecture_material: Hidden flaw of simple interest: 10% on 100 gives 10%, 9.09%, 5.26% in years 1, 2, 10; derivation of i_n = i/(1 + i(n-1)) (f0036); compound model earns the same rate each year; graph line against curve at 10% (f0039); the gap diverges.
sections.teaching_construction: Derivation of (1.6) from (1.3) and its domain 1 + i(n-1) > 0; compound i_n = i; the converse by induction (constant effective rate implies compound growth at whole periods); running case rates 8.0000%, 7.4074%, 6.8966%, 6.4516%.

sections.section: Periods shorter than one: the crossover
sections.lecture_material: Crossover trap 0 < t < 1: 6 months at 10%, simple 1.050 against compound 1.0488 (f0042); chord property of the convex compound curve (f0047); summary table (f0049); 9-month example 1,060.00 against 1,059.22 and the decision for simple interest (frame at 1497 s); advice: simple for short terms, compound for long terms.
sections.teaching_construction: Proposition (1.7) with a strict-convexity proof for every i > -1, i != 0 (including negative rates); Figure 1.1 at i = 100%; exact 9-month value 1,059.42; running case 100,000 at t = 0.75 (94,339.62 against 94,391.35); the hypotheses of the advice and the size of the advantage (0.000592 per unit at 7%, at t = 0.503).

sections.section: Moving money backward: the discount factor and present value
sections.lecture_material: Travelling backward in time; start x (1+i) = end with end = 1 gives v = 1/(1+i) (f0017); 100/1.05 = 95.23 handwritten; inverse logic box (f0018); move t years: multiply or divide by (1+i)^t, PV = FV v^t (f0021); BA II Plus tip 1.05, 1/x, 0.95238 (f0023).
sections.teaching_construction: Exact 95.24; v decreasing in i with dv/di < 0 and not inversely proportional; PV under simple interest FV/(1+it) and its difference from FV v^t by (1.7); running case v^4 = 0.735030 and 441,017.91.

sections.section: The effective rate of discount
sections.lecture_material: Haircut analogy: borrow 100, bank keeps 5, receive 95, repay 100 (f0028); d = interest/end = I_1/A(1) against i = interest/start (f0031); example i = 5/95 = 5.26%, d = 5% (f0035); derivation d = i/(1+i) = 1 - 1/(1+i) (f0040); d = iv (Identity 1, discount is PV of interest) and d = 1 - v (Identity 2) (f0043); triangle of rates (f0045); quiz i = 10%, d = 9.09% (f0049).
sections.teaching_construction: (1.10) valid under any accumulation function with a(1) = 1 + i; d_n = i_n/(1 + i_n); the readings of the two identities; running case discount reading 429,835.78 and 93,937.91; the distinction between a difference of model and a difference of rate.

sections.section: Why d is less than i, and the identities that link i, d and v
sections.lecture_material: Dual view: i on the start balance, d on the end balance (f0005); loan 100 to 110: i = 10%, d = 9.09%, proof d < i because FV > PV (f0012); i = d/(1-d) by two routes (f0021); v = 1 - d, PV = FV v^n = FV (1-d)^n (f0023); example 5,000 in 10 years at d = 6%, methods A and B, 2,692.83 (f0029); i - d = i - iv = i(1 - v) = id, a common true-or-false exam statement (f0033).
sections.teaching_construction: d < i for every i > -1, i != 0 from i - d = i^2/(1+i), including negative rates (i = -1% check); reading of i - d = id as interest on d; domain of (1.13) and the map from (-1, inf) onto (-inf, 1); exact 2,693.08 and Method A with 6.38% (2,693.83); running case i = 8.6957% under d = 8%, d = 7.4074% under i = 8%, and a loan with interest in advance (552,000).

sections.section: Solving for an unknown time: logarithms and the rule of 72
sections.lecture_material: (1+i)^n = 2; natural logs and ln(a^x) = x ln a; n ln(1+i) = ln 2; calculator 0.6931, 0.07696, 9.006 years (f0041); rule of 72: n = 72/(100 i), 9 years at 8%, accurate for 4% to 12% (f0043); summary of identities (f0046).
sections.research_extension: SOA Exam FM syllabus p. 1: specified calculators allowed; they remove the need to learn and be examined on certain approximation methods.
sections.teaching_construction: Domain of (1.15) and its meaning only under the fractional-time compound model; simple-interest doubling n = (g-1)/i (12.5 years at 8%); series derivation (1.16) n = 69.31/p + 0.347 - 0.000578 p + O(i^2) and the best-fit rate p = 7.8; proof that the relative error of the rule is strictly decreasing in i (derivative of ln(1+i)/i), so the three sampled rates bound the band 4% to 12% (at most 1.90%, 0.33 years at 4%, 0.12 years at 12%); Table 1.2 of errors (+3.36%, +1.85%, -0.07%, -1.90%, -7.28%); running case doubling 9.006 against 12.5 years.

sections.section: Practice: the basic time-value lab
sections.lecture_material: Lab protocol; doubling at 8% (9.006, rule 9) and at 10% (7.27, rule 7.2, band 4% to 12%) (f0024); equivalence trap 5% simple over 5 years, AV 1.25, compound 4.56% (f0039) and concept check (f0041); three cash flows at 6%, value at t = 3 = 2,282.82 (f0057), focal date, BA II Plus CF worksheet then multiply by 1.06^3 (f0059). Lecture 30 Question 1 option D, d = i/(1+i) (f0021).
sections.teaching_construction: Equivalent rate for any horizon T and the sign of j_T - i from (1.7); the equivalence holds at one horizon only (1.05 against 1.04564 at T = 1, and 1.50 against 1.5625 at T = 10); equation of value (1.17); independence of the focal date under compound interest; NPV 1,916.70 and the slide's calculator picture.

sections.section: The running case resolved
sections.lecture_material: None.
sections.teaching_construction: Table 1.1 (three readings of 8%, deposits for 600,000 at t = 4 and 100,000 at t = 0.75); the two separate choices (model: 13,527.54 and 51.72; rate: 11,182.14) and the spread 24,709.68; what generalizes and what is case-specific.

sections.section: Executable check of the definitions and the running case
sections.lecture_material: None.
sections.teaching_construction: Standard-library program: exact Fraction checks at i = 8/100 of (1.3) against (1.6) and against the constant i for n = 1..10, of d = iv = 1 - v, i - d = id and i = d/(1-d); floating-point grid check of (1.7) at six rates from -50% to 100%; running case, lecture examples and the rule-of-72 table; ValueError for i <= -1, t < 0, d >= 1, g <= 0 or i = 0 in (1.15); two failure tests described.

sections.section: What these models establish and what they do not
sections.lecture_material: Lecture 4 names Exam FM for i - d = id; Lecture 30 asks for Exam FM conditions.
sections.research_extension: SOA Exam FM syllabus p. 2: topic 1, Time Value of Money (5-15%), terms (simple and compound interest, accumulation function, present value, discount factor, rate of discount, effective rate) and outcome (b).
sections.teaching_construction: Classification into definitions, models and derivations; where the results stop applying (changing rates, mid-period cash flows, day count, simple discount against simple interest solved backward, focal-date dependence under simple interest, tiered rates, certainty).

sections.section: Exercises
sections.lecture_material: Exercise 3 extends the haircut loan of Lecture 3; Exercise 4 extends the lab's focal date; Exercise 6 extends the doubling-time problems of Lectures 4 and 5.
sections.teaching_construction: Six original exercises with full solutions: derive (i - d = id two ways, d < i for negative rates, interest on d), exam-style closest-of-five (present value at a rate of discount, each distractor tied to an error), check an assumption (discount-quoted against interest-quoted loan), counterexample (focal-date dependence and splitting under simple interest), design and judge (simple or compound by term, renewal, largest advantage), unknown time and the rule of 72 (factor 4, 18%, simple interest, rate of discount).

sections.section: The running case and the tools from earlier in the course
sections.lecture_material: Roadmap: distinguish effective and nominal rates, frequency of compounding, relation between i and i(m), conversion formulas; examples of compounding frequencies (quarterly, semi-annual, monthly; daily for credit cards).
sections.teaching_construction: Restatement, taken as given from earlier in the course, of a(t), A(t) = k a(t), the effective rate i = a(1) - 1, the compound model (2.1), v, d and 1 + i = (1 - d)^-1 (2.2); the rounding rule; the running case (500,000 repaid in one sum after 5 years; four invented quotes A-D) and the formal model (a year cut into m periods, a rate charged at the end or the start of each, the growth factor of the year).

sections.section: A quoted rate and an earned rate: the bank advertisement
sections.lecture_material: Bank advertisement 12% compounded monthly; 1% a month, interest on interest; (1.01)^12 = 1.1268, effective 12.68% (f0014).
sections.teaching_construction: Exact value 12.6825%; 10,000 earns 1,268.25 against 1,200; the assumption that monthly interest is left in the account.

sections.section: Nominal rate of interest, frequency and periodic rate
sections.lecture_material: Effective rate i, nominal rate i(m) (name-only rate), frequency m (f0021); trap alert: the superscript is a label, not an exponent; golden rule: effective rate per period = i(m)/m, i(12) = 12% gives 1% (f0025); periodic rate as 'the real engine' (summary f0067); synonyms compounded, convertible, payable monthly all mean i(12) = 0.12 (f0060, L6 about 1752-1798 s).
sections.teaching_construction: Numerical contrast i^12 = 10^-12 against i(12) = 9.5690% at 10%; definition (2.3) labelled as a convention; the book symbol j = i(m)/m; i(1) = i.

sections.section: The bridge equation for nominal interest
sections.lecture_material: Path A a(1) = 1 + i; path B compounding m times, period by period with the common factor 1 + i(m)/m; fundamental link 1 + i = (1 + i(m)/m)^m and i = (1 + i(m)/m)^m - 1 (f0033).
sections.teaching_construction: Inverse (2.5) and its reading as m times the effective rate per period; checks m = 1, the advertisement, round trip, zero rate; running case offers B (10.0339%, 806,495.47) and C (10.0401%, 806,723.83); boundary (reinvestment, 1 + i(m)/m > 0, interest between period ends).

sections.section: The frequency of compounding at a fixed nominal rate
sections.lecture_material: Nominal fixed at 12%: annual 12.00%, semi-annual 12.36%, quarterly 12.55%, monthly 12.68%, daily 12.747%; conclusion: as m increases, effective i increases (f0039).
sections.teaching_construction: Table 2.1 to four decimals; the chord lemma with proof; proof of monotonicity in m for every m via the chord property of ln(1 + xy); limit (2.6) (1 + x/m)^m -> e^x with the cap e^0.12 - 1 = 12.7497% and the bound e^x - 1 - x; the opposite behaviour of discount quotes noted.

sections.section: A nominal rate for a given effective rate, and the calculator worksheet
sections.lecture_material: Problem: i(4) equivalent to i = 10%; fourth root, isolate, multiply by 4 (f0047); printed solution 1.02411, 0.02411, 9.64% and calculator 9.65 (f0053); BA II Plus ICONV worksheet: 2nd and 2, NOM, EFF, C/Y (f0050).
sections.research_extension: TI BA II PLUS guidebook p. 61: worksheet variables NOM, EFF, C/Y; NOM defined as rate per compounding period times periods per year; equal nominal rates with different compounding periods are not comparable without conversion to EFF. p. 62: 15% compounded quarterly gives EFF 15.87.
sections.teaching_construction: Unrounded 9.6455%; the 2.41% error of omitting the factor 4; explanation of the slide's 9.64 against 9.65; 15.8650% for the guidebook example; keystrokes labelled an evaluation, not a derivation.

sections.section: Growth over t years, and the words for compounding
sections.lecture_material: N = m t periods; A(t) = k (1 + i(m)/m)^(mt); example 1000 for 5 years at 8% quarterly: 20 periods, 2%, 1000 (1.02)^20 = 1485.95 (f0057); synonyms of compounded (f0060).
sections.teaching_construction: Equivalence of (2.7) and (2.1); the case of non-whole mt (model against a bank's crediting rule); effective 8.2432% for the example; running case amounts for A, B, C; the ambiguity of a quote with no frequency.

sections.section: The ordering of the nominal rates of interest
sections.lecture_material: For fixed effective i > 0: i(1) > i(2) > i(4) > i(12) > ...; the more powerful the compounding, the lower the required nominal rate (f0063); credit-card remark (speech); summary (f0067); next lecture: discount rates in advance.
sections.teaching_construction: Values at 10%; the link to the monotonicity of the previous section; the proof deferred to the hierarchy section; the credit-card remark graded as the speaker's judgment.

sections.section: Nominal rate of discount: interest taken in advance m times a year
sections.lecture_material: Roadmap (f0005); recall nominal interest paid at the end of every period; nominal discount d(m): interest taken in advance at the start of every period, m times a year; loan of 100 with 5 taken in advance; haircut: d(12) = 12% is 1% at the start of every month (f0014); Golden Rule 2: effective discount per period d(m)/m, the factor moves money backward 1/m year (f0017).
sections.teaching_construction: Definition (2.8) as the value 1 - d(m)/m at the start of a period of 1 due at its end; the 1% as a fraction of the end amount, 1.0101% of the amount handed over; d(1) = d; the condition d(m)/m < 1.

sections.section: The bridge equation for discount
sections.lecture_material: Present value of 1 over a full year: path A v = 1 - d, path B discounting m times v = (1 - d(m)/m)^m; fundamental link 1 - d = (1 - d(m)/m)^m; the memory aid +i against -d (f0018, f0025).
sections.teaching_construction: The step-back argument for path B; the second form 1 + i = (1 - d(m)/m)^-m; inverse (2.10) and its reading; checks m = 1, i = 0, d(12) = 12% gives 12.8178% against 12.6825%; running case offer D (10.0920%, 808,628.54); boundary (discount on the end amount, d(m)/m < 1, not a day-proportional discount).

sections.section: Converting between frequencies: the master equation
sections.lecture_material: Since v = (1 + i)^-1, the master equation (1 - d(p)/p)^-p = 1 + i = (1 + i(m)/m)^m with p and m possibly different; power: convert discount monthly to interest quarterly without finding i first (f0029, f0040).
sections.teaching_construction: Equivalence of quotes as equality of 1 + i; direct conversion d(12) = 6% to i(4) = 6.0605% with the exponent -3, and the check through i = 6.1996%; the running case restated as i(12): 9.5690, 9.6000, 9.6057, 9.6533.

sections.section: The hierarchy of rates
sections.lecture_material: Number line with d at the left and i at the right; as m increases the rates move inward; inequality chain d < d(2) < d(4) < ... < i(4) < i(2) < i (f0039); values at 10%: d 9.09, d(2) 9.31, d(4) 9.42, d(12) 9.49, i(12) 9.57, i(4) 9.65, i(2) 9.76 (f0046); the rates converge to a central value, named in the recording as the force of interest treated later.
sections.teaching_construction: Table 2.2 to four decimals with m = 52, 365; d(1) = d and i(1) = i; application of the chord lemma; proof of (2.13) for every m, p and every i > -1, i != 0, with the common limit ln(1 + i); conditions (i = 0 collapses; strictness needs m > 1); 365-thly values 9.5298% and 9.5323%; interpretation by timing within the year.

sections.section: A nominal rate of discount from an effective rate of interest
sections.lecture_material: Problem: d(4) equivalent to i = 6%; route through d = 0.06/1.06 = 0.0566; direct route (1 - d(4)/4)^-4 = 1.06, power -1/4, 0.9855, 0.01446, 5.78% (f0061); trap alert: ICONV handles only i(m), not d(m) (f0062).
sections.research_extension: TI BA II PLUS guidebook p. 61: ICONV variables NOM, EFF, C/Y (no rate of discount).
sections.teaching_construction: Unrounded 5.7847%; agreement of the two routes; explanation of 0.01446 against 0.0145; check of (2.13) at 6% (5.6604 < 5.7847 < 5.8269 < 5.8695 < 6).

sections.section: The same frequency: an identity linking the two nominal rates
sections.lecture_material: For m = p: i(m)/m - d(m)/m = (i(m)/m)(d(m)/m), or 1 + i(m)/m = (1 - d(m)/m)^-1, the periodic version of 1 + i = (1 - d)^-1 (f0065); i - d = id for effective rates (speech); summary of notation table a(1) for i, d, i(m), d(m) (f0069); d(m) < i(m) (f0071).
sections.teaching_construction: Derivation of (2.14) from (2.11); reciprocal identity (2.15) 1/d(m) - 1/i(m) = 1/m with the check at 10%, m = 12; d(m) = i(m)/(1 + i(m)/m) and its reading; second proof of d(m) < i(m); exact check at i(12) = 12% (d(12) = 11.8812%).

sections.section: A discount rate in a market quotation: Treasury bills
sections.lecture_material: US Treasury bills and commercial paper quoted by discount rates; one-year bill at 5.125% as an annualized discount rate on a 360-day year; pricing deferred to Module 2 (f0067); closing summary and preview of continuous compounding (f0071).
sections.research_extension: TreasuryDirect, Understanding Pricing and Interest Rates, section Bills: price = face (1 - discount rate x time/360), example 26-week bill at 0.145% priced 999.27.
sections.teaching_construction: (2.16) as simple discount on a 360-day year, contrasted with compound d(m); 182/360 = 0.50556 against 1/2; the lecture's bill at 364 days: price 94.8181, effective 5.4806% on a 365-day year (a labelled construction); the three sources of the 0.36-point gap.

sections.section: The running case resolved
sections.lecture_material: None.
sections.teaching_construction: Table 2.3 (quote, growth factor, effective rate, rate restated as i(12), amount owed); D costs 3,373.54 more than A (0.42% of A's amount, 1.1% of A's interest 305,255.00); the reversal explained by (2.13); what generalizes (the conversion procedure) and what is case-specific (the gaps).

sections.section: Executable check of the conversions and the running case
sections.lecture_material: None.
sections.teaching_construction: Standard-library program: exact Fraction checks of (2.4) = (2.9) at i(12) = 12% with d(12) from (2.14), and of (2.14), (2.15); strict chain (2.13) and round trips of (2.4), (2.5), (2.9), (2.10) within 1e-12 at i = 10% and -10% for eight frequencies; lecture, guidebook and TreasuryDirect examples; running case; ValueError for a non-whole or non-positive m and a non-positive growth factor; two failure tests run.

sections.section: What these formulas establish and what they do not
sections.lecture_material: None.
sections.research_extension: SOA Exam FM syllabus p. 2, learning outcome 1(c): conversion among the effective interest rate, nominal interest rate convertible m-thly, effective discount rate, nominal discount rate convertible m-thly and the force of interest.
sections.teaching_construction: Classification of the assumptions (definitions, a constant compound-rate model, a quotation convention); what the program tests and what only the proofs establish; where the formulas stop applying (changing rates, crediting rules for fractions of a period, unstated frequency, day-count discounts).

sections.section: Exercises
sections.lecture_material: Exercise 2 extends the d(4) example of Lecture 7; Exercise 5(a) uses the master equation of Lecture 7; Exercise 6 applies the Treasury-bill case of Lecture 7.
sections.research_extension: Exercise 6 uses the TreasuryDirect pricing formula.
sections.teaching_construction: Six original exercises with full solutions: derive (same-frequency identity, reciprocal identity, d(m) = i(m)/(1 + i(m)/m)), exam-style closest-of-five (a nominal discount rate, each distractor tied to an error), check an assumption (a quote with no frequency, four readings), counterexample and proof (frequency raises the cost of an interest quote and lowers that of a discount quote), design and judgment (direct conversion i(4) to d(12); two deposits compared), trap (a market discount rate read as d(2)).

sections.section: The running case and the tools from earlier in the course
sections.lecture_material: Recap of i, d, v, nominal rates i(m) and d(m) and their links to 1 + i; discrete compounding moves in steps; plan: from discrete m to continuous, define delta, derive 1 + i = e^delta, connect delta to i(m) and d(m).
sections.teaching_construction: Restatement, taken as given from earlier in the course, of A(t) = A(0) a(t) with a(0) = 1 (3.1), compound interest (1+i)^t for real t, v and d, and the equivalences (3.2) and (3.3); the rounding convention; the running case (four invented offers quoted as 8%, a second deposit at t = 2, a target of 200,000 at t = 5); the formal model (accumulation function and its rate of growth).

sections.section: From nominal rates to the force of interest
sections.lecture_material: As m increases money grows faster; Euler's limit (1 + 1/n)^n -> e and its generalization (1 + r/m)^m -> e^r; i(m) -> delta as m -> infinity, written i(infinity); definition: delta is the nominal annual rate of interest compounded continuously; result 1 + i = lim (1 + delta/m)^m = e^delta.
sections.teaching_construction: Separation of the fixed-nominal and fixed-effective questions, with the proof that (1 + q/m)^m increases in m and the numbers 1.104713 and 1.105171; values of i(m) at 10% falling with m; definition (3.4) and the derivation of delta = ln(1+i) from (e^u - 1)/u -> 1; d(m) -> delta; relation (3.5); lemma (3.6) with proof for a convergent sequence, which completes the slide's route; interpretation and boundary.

sections.section: Converting between i and the force: steps and a ramp
sections.lecture_material: Staircase (annual compounding) against smooth ramp (continuous); at t = 1 equivalent rates reach the same height 1 + i; the slide's 10% staircase and e^(0.1t) are not equivalent; delta = ln(1+i); trap alert: delta slightly less than i, ln 1.10 = 9.53%.
sections.teaching_construction: Figure 3.1 with the equivalent curve 1.1^t and the gap 1.105171 against 1.10; the staircase as the model (1+i)^floor(t), different from (1+i)^t between year ends (1.153690 against 1.10 at t = 1.5); conversion in both directions; size of the gap; banks A and C converted (0.076961; 8.3287%).

sections.section: Accumulation and discounting under a constant force
sections.lecture_material: a(t) = (1+i)^t = e^(delta t); FV = PV e^(delta t), PV = FV e^(-delta t); delta = 0 gives i = 0; doubling at constant force 5%: e^(0.05t) = 2, t = ln 2/0.05 = 0.6931/0.05 = 13.86 years.
sections.teaching_construction: Units of delta t; v = e^(-delta); comparison with doubling at effective 5% (14.2067 years, gap 0.3438; effective equivalent 5.1271%); running case banks A (146,932.81) and C (149,182.47), difference 2,249.66; boundary.

sections.section: Where the force sits among the other rates
sections.lecture_material: Maclaurin series ln(1+i) = i - i^2/2 + i^3/3 - ...; delta approximately i - i^2/2 'confirms' delta < i, for positive or negative i; grand inequality d < d(m) < delta < i(m) < i for m > 1 on a number line, delta 'the perfect center'; Example 2: d(4) = 8%, (1 - 0.08/4)^(-4) = 1 + i = e^delta, delta = -4 ln 0.98 = 8.08%; the skill called important for Exam FM; summary (delta sits strictly between d(m) and i(m)).
sections.research_extension: SOA Exam FM syllabus p. 2: force of interest among the defined terms; conversion among i, i(m), d, d(m) and the force of interest.
sections.teaching_construction: Truncation error 0.000310 at 10%; proof of delta < i from e^y > 1 + y, including i = -5% (delta = -0.051293); proof of (3.8) from the integral representations (3.9), with monotonicity of i(m) and d(m) in m and their common limit; Table 3.1; the perfect-center metaphor graded, midpoint 0.095455 against 0.095310 and the i^3/6 difference; the full chain for d(4) = 8% (0.077632 < 0.08 < 0.080811 < 0.081633 < 0.084166); bank B 149,788.50 and the ranking B, C, A by force.

sections.section: The force at an instant
sections.lecture_material: Motivation: previous lectures had constant i or delta and growth e^(delta t); real world: rates fluctuate, central banks change rates, market volatility (speaker's illustration); can delta_t be negative (question left open); derivation from i(4)/4 = [A(t + 1/4) - A(t)]/A(t), i(m) = m [A(t + 1/m) - A(t)]/A(t), m = 1/h, limit A'(t)/A(t) = delta_t = d/dt ln A(t); A(t) = k a(t). Lecture 8 slide 11 (f0057) states the calculus definition and its interpretation as the relative rate of change.
sections.teaching_construction: Assumptions of the derivation (A differentiable, A > 0); independence of the investment size; interest over a short interval A(t) delta_t h + o(h), daily example 21.92; units; checks: compound interest gives constant ln(1+i), simple interest gives i/(1 + it) (0.08 to 0.057143); negative force answered; boundary (no force at credit dates of a staircase).

sections.section: From the force to the accumulation function
sections.lecture_material: Integrate delta_r = d/dr ln a(r) from 0 to t: ln a(t) - ln a(0); a(0) = 1; master equation a(t) = exp(integral_0^t delta_r dr); delta is a function of time, location matters; to move from t1 to t2 integrate from t1 to t2, not from 0 to t2 - t1; AV = PV exp(integral_t1^t2 delta_r dr).
sections.teaching_construction: Differential equation (3.11); uniqueness proof via (b e^(-Delta))' = 0, positivity for any sign of the force; checks for constant force and simple interest; (3.13) from (3.1) and (3.12); the average force and its equivalent effective rate.

sections.section: Area under the force, and the integration-limit trap
sections.lecture_material: Integral as the area under delta_t, accumulation factor e^(area), intervals [1,2] and [2,3] have different areas; Example 1: delta_t = 0.01t, 100 invested for 5 years, integral 0.125, AV = 100 e^0.125 = 113.31; trap alert: deposit at t = 2, value at t = 5, correct exp(integral_2^5), wrong exp(integral_0^3); shape matters, time is absolute.
sections.teaching_construction: Trap quantified for 0.01t (0.105 against 0.045; 1.110711 against 1.046028); shift formula beta t1 (t2 - t1) for a linear force; proof that the shortcut holds for all dates only for a constant force; Figure 3.2; running case bank D: a(t) = exp(0.06t + 0.004t^2), same a(5) as C, a(2.5) 1.191246 against 1.221403, second deposit 65,106.41 against C 63,562.46 and trap 62,055.12 (3,051.29 short), exponent gap 0.048, average force 0.088 (9.1988%).

sections.section: A force that jumps: step functions
sections.lecture_material: delta_t = 0.04 for 0 <= t < 3 and 0.06 for 3 <= t <= 5; value of 1 at t = 5; split the integral at 3, a single point contributes nothing; rectangles 0.12 + 0.12 = 0.24; AV = e^0.24 = 1.2712; draw delta_t to find split points.
sections.teaching_construction: Continuity argument: a continuous at the jump, (3.12) on each piece joined by (3.13), a(5) = e^0.12 e^0.12; no derivative at t = 3 (one-sided slopes); equivalent effective rates 4.0811% and 6.1837% and the rounded-factor product 1.271251; average force 0.048; one-panel Simpson across the jump gives 0.216667.

sections.section: From the accumulation function back to the force
sections.teaching_construction: Check by (3.12) with substitution: integral 0 to 2 = ln 1.2 = 0.182322; difference-quotient check in the program; the force rises and falls (0, 0.166667, 0.222222, 0.166667 at t = 0, 2, 4, 10) although a increases; boundary (a differentiable, positive, a(0) = 1).

sections.section: Discounting with a variable force
sections.lecture_material: FV = PV exp(integral_0^T delta_r dr); multiply both sides by e^(-a); PV = FV exp(-integral_0^T delta_r dr); the integral as the total resistance or cost of time; summary: v(t) = exp(-integral_0^t delta_r dr), always integrate over [t1, t2]; next lecture: real and nominal rates, Fisher equation.
sections.teaching_construction: (3.14) with v(t) = 1/a(t) and v(t) = v^t for constant force; discounting between t1 and t2; the metaphor restated as the logarithm of the accumulation factor; running case PV 134,064.01 under D, 136,116.64 under A, 153,594.71 at t = 2 under D; focal-date independence under a variable force.

sections.section: The running case resolved
sections.lecture_material: None.
sections.teaching_construction: Table 3.2 with the four offers, the second deposit under C, D and the wrong limits, and the target deposit; differences 606.04, 2,855.70 and 1,543.95; the reversal caused by wrong limits; what generalizes (the procedure) and what is case-specific (the invented forces).

sections.section: Executable check of the formulas and the running case
sections.lecture_material: None.
sections.teaching_construction: Standard-library program: nominal rates at 10% for m = 1, 4, 12, 365, 10^6 and an assertion of (3.8) for m = 2..998; the lecture examples, with exact Fraction integrals (1/8, 6/25) by Simpson's rule, which is exact for cubics; the one-panel Simpson value across the jump; delta_2 by a central difference; assertions that a constant force reproduces 1.08^5 (1e-12) and that the simple-interest force integrates to ln 1.4 (1e-9); the running case with exponents 33/125 and 27/125; ValueError for i <= -1, t1 > t2, gaps or incomplete cover, odd or non-positive n; two failure tests described.

sections.section: What these results establish and what they do not
sections.lecture_material: Lecture 8 names Exam FM.
sections.research_extension: SOA Exam FM syllabus p. 2: force of interest, conversions, and time-value equations involving variable force of interest.
sections.teaching_construction: Classification of the results (theorems from (3.6), (3.9), (3.11)) and of the assumptions (definitions, a deterministic continuous-growth model, a unit convention); where the results stop applying (discrete crediting, no single delta for a varying force, dependence on dates, no claim about actual rate paths).

sections.section: Exercises
sections.lecture_material: Exercise 3 restates the idea of the Lecture 30 Q1 statements for a step force; Exercises 2, 4, 5 and 6 extend the linear-force, step-force, discounting and inversion examples of Lecture 9.
sections.teaching_construction: Six original exercises with full solutions: derive (force of simple discount against simple interest), exam-style closest-of-five (linear force, deposit at t = 1, each distractor tied to an error), check an assumption (five statements for a step force), counterexample and proof (order of step pieces), computation with two focal dates and a trap, inversion and judgment (maximum of the force of 1 + 0.05t^2).

sections.section: The running case and the tools from earlier in the course
sections.lecture_material: Recap of weeks 1-3: moving a single cash flow from 0 to n (future value) and from n to 0 (present value), focal date and equation of value; week 4 turns to streams of regular payments; geometric series as the tool.
sections.teaching_construction: Restatement, taken as given from earlier in the course, of the effective rate i, accumulation and discounting (7.1), v, d = iv = 1 - v and v(1+i) = 1 (7.2), the equation of value and the independence of the focal date under one constant rate, and the geometric series sum (7.3) with its subtraction step; the rounding convention (intermediate values unrounded, displayed factors rounded, with the largest resulting difference); the running case (saver from 30 to 65, income of 4,000 a month from 65 to 90, invented effective rates 6% and 4%); the formal model (timeline, level payments, rate, valuation date).

sections.section: What an annuity is, and the timing of an annuity-immediate
sections.lecture_material: Annuity = series of payments at equal intervals (examples: monthly mortgage payments, monthly pension cheques, semi-annual bond coupons); annuity-immediate pays at the end of each period, annuity-due at the start; the immediate trap: immediate does not mean now, first payment at t = 1, last at t = n (salary analogy); timeline with payments of 1 at 1, 2, ..., n.
sections.teaching_construction: Level and certain payments stated as part of the definition; Figure 7.1 (both timelines with the valuation dates of PV and AV); the rule that a value is incomplete without its valuation date.

sections.section: Present value of an annuity-immediate
sections.lecture_material: PV at t = 0 of payments of 1: v + v^2 + ... + v^n; geometric series with a = v, r = v, n terms; a angle n = v(1 - v^n)/(1 - v); multiply numerator and denominator by (1 + i); v(1+i) = 1 gives numerator 1 - v^n, (1 - v)(1 + i) = i gives denominator i; a angle n = (1 - v^n)/i.
sections.teaching_construction: Direct reading 1 - v = iv; loan interpretation 1 = i a + v^n; PMT a angle n for level payment PMT; small-rate expansion a = n - i n(n+1)/2 + O(i^2) with the check 9.999945 at n = 10, i = 1e-6; bounds a < n and a < 1/i; exact direct-sum check at 4%; running case first version 48,000 a angle 25 at 4% = 749,859.84; boundary of the formula.

sections.section: Worked examples and the calculator worksheet
sections.lecture_material: BA II Plus setup (P/Y = 1 for annual problems, clear TVM), the five keys N, I/Y, PV, PMT, FV and the sign convention (PV inflow, PMT outflow); demonstration PV 500, 5 years, 5% gives PMT 115.49; car loan 5,000 a year for 4 years at 6% = 17,325.53; investment of 1,000 a year for 10 years at 5% = 7,721.73, first payment worth 952 and last 614 today.
sections.research_extension: TI BA II PLUS guidebook p. 21: sign convention, END = ordinary annuity.
sections.teaching_construction: Keystrokes labelled a method of evaluating (7.4), not a derivation, dependent on P/Y, C/Y and END/BGN; check of 115.49 by (7.4); exact values 952.38 and 613.91 and their reading as the cost today of each payment.

sections.section: Solving for an unknown term or an unknown rate
sections.lecture_material: 10,000 at 5% with withdrawals of 1,000 a year: 1.05^-n = 0.5, n about 14.2, 14 full withdrawals and one smaller one, calculator 14.21; loan 5,000 repaid by 1,000 a year for 6 years: a angle 6 = 5, no algebraic isolation of i, calculator 5.47%.
sections.research_extension: SOA Exam FM syllabus p. 3: drop and balloon payments named as final-payment conventions for loans.
sections.teaching_construction: n = ln 2/ln 1.05 = 14.2067; drop payment B = 210.72 at t = 15 and balloon 1,200.68 at t = 14, against 206.70 from the fractional part; uniqueness proof of the rate root (continuous strictly decreasing f with a sign change) and the case n PMT <= PV with no positive root; bisection with tolerance 1e-12 and 40 halvings from [1e-9, 1]; root 5.4718% and its check; condition of one sign change.

sections.section: The annuity-due: the same payments one period earlier
sections.lecture_material: Annuity-due: payments at the start of each period, first at t = 0, last at t = n - 1 (rent, insurance); shift left; each payment earns one extra period, value due = value immediate x (1 + i); notation a double-dot angle n; = (1 - v^n)/d with i/(1+i) = d; tip to multiply by (1 + i) instead of memorizing; BGN keystrokes (2nd BGN, 2nd SET, 2nd QUIT); apartment lease 1,000 a month in advance for a year at 1% a month: 11,255.08 x 1.01 = 11,367.63; lottery 50,000 today against 10,000 a year for 6 years from today at 6%: 5.2124, 52,124, better by 2,124; trap slide: forgetting to switch back to END.
sections.research_extension: TI BA II PLUS guidebook p. 21: END for ordinary annuities (most loans), BGN for annuities due (most leases).
sections.teaching_construction: Term-by-term derivation of (7.5); timeline derivation (7.6) a-due = 1 + a angle n-1 and its agreement with (7.5); exact check at 4%, n = 25 (16.246963); running case second version 48,000 a-due angle 25 = 779,854.23 and the 29,994.39 (3.8%) under-funding from the wrong timing; exact lottery values 52,123.64 and 2,123.64; the Exam FM remark graded as the speaker's judgment.

sections.section: Accumulated value of an annuity-immediate and its valuation date
sections.lecture_material: Saver's perspective; s angle n = accumulated value at the time of the last payment; first payment grows n - 1 years, last earns nothing; FV = 1 + (1+i) + ... + (1+i)^(n-1); geometric series with a = 1, r = 1 + i; s angle n = ((1+i)^n - 1)/i; golden link s = a (1+i)^n with the loan-versus-saving reading; retirement goal 5,000 a year for 30 years at 7%: 5000 x 94.4608 = 472,304, deposits 150,000, interest 322,304, calculator 472,303.93; millionaire goal 1,000,000 in 20 years at 8%: s = 45.762, PMT 21,852.17, due 49.423 and 20,233.50; valuation-date trap: save 10 years, wait 5, value s angle 10 (1+i)^5, not s angle 15. Lecture 16 (1733-1816 s) previews s angle n and the link.
sections.teaching_construction: Algebraic check of (7.9); limits s -> n as i -> 0 and s > n; interest ratio 2.15 to 1; exact deposit 21,852.21 and the rounding rule; running case third version: annual deposit 6,998.30 to the goal 779,854.23 (the second version's fund); trap quantified at 7% (19.378283 against 25.129022, 30% too large).

sections.section: Accumulated value of an annuity-due
sections.lecture_material: s double-dot = s x (1 + i) = ((1+i)^n - 1)/d; logic check: last deposit at t = n - 1 has one full year before valuation at t = n; unknown term in BGN mode: wrong way s = 20, right way s-due = 20, P/Y = C/Y = 1, I/Y = 6, PMT = -5000, FV = 100,000, PV = 0 gives 12.9931; reset to END.
sections.teaching_construction: Placement note (section after the L18 section because it uses s angle n); s-due = (1+i)^n a-due; the valuation-date trap for the due type; n = 12.9931 from 1.06^n = 2.132075; 12 deposits worth 89,410.69 at t = 12, 13 worth 100,075.33 at t = 13, a reduced 13th deposit of 4,928.93; running case fourth version: annual deposit 6,602.17 to the goal 779,854.23.

sections.section: Annuities payable m-thly
sections.lecture_material: Payments m times a year (12 monthly, 4 quarterly) with annual rates; bread-slicer picture; a(m) angle n = PV of a total of 1 per year paid in instalments of 1/m at the end of each m-th of a year, nm payments; warning: 100 a month means 1,200 x a(12); denominator slot machine: numerator 1 - v^n, denominator i, d, i(m), and d(m) for the m-thly due (speech); bridge equation (1 + i(m)/m)^m = 1 + i; monthly payout 100 a month for 5 years at effective 6%: i(12) = 0.05841, PV 5,192.38; P/Y hazard slide (P/Y = 12, C/Y = 12, N = 60, I/Y = 5.841, or the annual rate if P/Y matches C/Y), reset P/Y; car loan 20,000 at 400 a month, 6% nominal monthly: 57.68 months, 57 full payments and a drop payment at month 58; s(m) = a(m)(1+i)^n = ((1+i)^n - 1)/i(m), accumulation factor stays annual.
sections.research_extension: TI BA II PLUS guidebook p. 21 (P/Y sets C/Y unless changed) and p. 69 (rate per payment period (1 + I/Y/(100 C/Y))^(C/Y/P/Y) - 1).
sections.teaching_construction: Definition of j and of i(m) (7.11) and d(m) (7.14); derivations of a(m) (7.12)-(7.13), a-due(m) (7.15) and s(m) (7.16) from geometric series; the device placed after the derivation as a mnemonic with its limits; limits i -> 0, m -> infinity and n -> infinity of the m-thly values (7.13), (7.15), (7.16); the ordering a < a(m) < a-due(m) < a-due with values at 4%; the slide's calculator alternative gives 5,172.56, and C/Y = 1 with P/Y = 12 enters an effective rate; exact drop payment 272.27 against 0.68 x 400; running case monthly version: d(12) = 0.039157, fund 766,009.45, s(12) angle 35 at 6% = 114.466998, deposit 557.66 (unrounded 557.664; the rounded deposit builds 766,003.99, 5.46 short), totals 234,218.87 (420 times the unrounded deposit; 420 x 557.66 = 234,217.20) and 1,200,000.

sections.section: Two phases on one timeline: the retirement-planning lab
sections.lecture_material: Lab: retire at 65, live to 90, need 5,000 a month at the start of each month at 4%; PV65 = 12 x 5000 x a-due(12) angle 25 at 4%; calculator BGN, P/Y = C/Y = 12, N = 300, I/Y = 4: 950,419.96; saving from 25 for 40 years at 8%, end of month, END mode: 272.25; waiting until 45: 1,613.56 and a six-fold burden; unified equation of value at the retirement date with different phase rates; early-retirement exercise: 2,000 a month for 20 years at 7%, 4,000 a month for 30 years at 5%, both at the end of the month: assets 1.04 million, liabilities 745,126.47, surplus 296,000; inflation as the missing factor.
sections.research_extension: TI BA II PLUS guidebook p. 69 (I/Y with C/Y = 12 is a monthly rate I/Y/1200) and p. 21 (P/Y sets C/Y).
sections.teaching_construction: Equation (7.17) with the timing reason for s(12) and a-due(12) at the same date; Figure 7.2; the two readings of I/Y = 4: nominal 4% convertible monthly (effective 4.0742%) reproduces 950,419.96, effective 4% gives 957,511.81 (+7,091.86, 0.75%); effective 8% deposit 295.06 (+8.4%); ratio 5.93; exact surplus 296,726.85; the subscript remark on the f0035 formula.
